-212.d: Qin's territory reaches its greatest extent (c. 214–210 BC). In the north Meng Tian leads three hundred thousand men to drive out the Xiongnu and take Henandi, sets up Jiuyuan Commandery, uses the river as a barrier and joins the old long walls of Qin, Zhao and Yan into the Great Wall, and builds the Straight Road from Yunyang to Jiuyuan; in the south Tu Sui, Ren Xiao and Zhao Tuo campaign against the Hundred Yue, the supervising censor Lu cuts the Lingqu Canal as a supply route, Lingnan is pacified, and the Nanhai, Guilin and Xiang commanderies are set up. The imperial highways reach across the realm, and the interior long walls and forts between the six states are torn down ("pulling down city walls … levelling strongholds") and abandoned.

-221.d: Wang Ben attacks Qi southward from Yan, and Jian, king of Qi, surrenders. King Zheng of Qin takes the title "First Emperor" and divides the realm into thirty-six commanderies, with a standard script, a standard axle gauge and unified weights and measures. Wey survives as a dependency until 209 BC.

-222.d: Wang Ben attacks Liaodong and captures Xi, king of Yan, then turns on Dai and captures Jia, king of Dai; Wang Jian pacifies Chu's lands south of the Yangtze, receives the surrender of the lords of Yue and sets up Kuaiji Commandery.
-222.t: Fall of Yan and Dai · Jiangnan pacified

-223.d: Wang Jian and Meng Wu crush Chu at Qinan; Xiang Yan dies, and Fuchu, king of Chu, is captured.

-224.d: Li Xin and Meng Tian invade Chu with two hundred thousand men and are routed by Xiang Yan at Chengfu; the king of Qin recalls Wang Jian, who invades Chu with six hundred thousand men and takes the land from Chen south to Pingyu.

-225.d: Wang Ben floods Daliang with water from the He and the Honggou for three months; the walls give way, Jia, king of Wei, surrenders, and Wei falls.

-226.d: After Jing Ke's attempt on the king of Qin fails (227 BC), Wang Jian crushes the allied Yan and Dai armies west of the Yi River and takes Ji, the Yan capital; Xi, king of Yan, falls back to Liaodong and beheads Crown Prince Dan to appease Qin.

-228.d: Qin sows discord and Qian, king of Zhao, has Li Mu killed; Wang Jian crushes Zhao and captures King Qian at Handan; Prince Jia of Zhao flees to Dai with his clan and makes himself king of Dai.

-230.d: The Neishi Teng attacks Han, captures An, king of Han, and makes Han's land Yingchuan Commandery. Qin's war of unification formally begins.

-233.d: Li Mu crushes the Qin army at Fei (233 BC) and again at Powu the next year, holding back Qin for the time being; Han Fei goes to Qin as envoy and dies at Yunyang.

-236.d: Wei has ceded Ye to Zhao (239 BC); the Qin generals Wang Jian, Huan Yi and Yang Duanhe attack Zhao and take Ye, Yuyu and seven other towns. With the revolt of Lao Ai (238 BC) put down, King Zheng of Qin has taken personal charge of government.

-241.d: Qin has taken Suanzao and nineteen other Wei towns and set up Dong Commandery (242 BC), cutting the north–south links of the states east of the mountains, and the lord of Wey is moved to Yewang; the last five-state vertical alliance against Qin is defeated at Zui; Chu moves its capital to Shouchun.

-247.d: Lord Xinling leads the armies of five states to crush Meng Ao at Hewai and pursues him to Hangu Pass; Qin retakes Shangdang and first sets up Taiyuan Commandery; the same year Zheng, king of Qin, comes to the throne.

-249.d: The Qin chancellor Lü Buwei destroys East Zhou; Qin takes Chenggao and Xingyang from Han and sets up Sanchuan Commandery, and Qin's lands now reach Daliang in Wei.

-256.d: Qin destroys West Zhou, King Nan of Zhou dies, and the Nine Tripods go to Qin; King Kaolie of Chu takes Lu (destroying it in 249 BC). Around this time Li Bing directs the building of Dujiangyan.
-256.t: Death of King Nan of Zhou

-257.d: Qin besieges Handan for nearly three years; Lord Xinling of Wei steals the tally to rescue Zhao and Lord Chunshen of Chu comes to Zhao's aid, and the Qin army is routed; Zhao recovers some of the Shangdang towns, and Qin takes Ningxinzhong from Wei.

-260.d: Zhao replaces Lian Po with Zhao Kuo, who attacks and is surrounded; after forty-six days without food he is killed; more than four hundred thousand surrendered troops are buried alive. Yiqu has already been destroyed by Qin, and Qin holds all of Shangdang.

-262.d: Bai Qi of Qin takes Yewang from Han, cutting Shangdang off from the Han heartland; Feng Ting, governor of Shangdang, surrenders its seventeen towns to Zhao, and a decisive war between Qin and Zhao is imminent.

-266.d: Fan Ju becomes chancellor of Qin and advocates "ally with the distant, attack the near"; Qin takes Huai and Xingqiu from Wei, turning its spearhead on the Three Jin. Before this Zhao She has routed the Qin army at Yuyu (269 BC).
-266.t: Ally with the distant, attack the near

-272.d: Queen Dowager Xuan of Qin lures the king of Yiqu to his death, Qin destroys Yiqu and builds a long wall against the Hu; before this Qin has taken Wu and Qianzhong from Chu (277 BC), and Bai Qi has crushed Wei and Zhao at Huayang (273 BC); this year Nanyang Commandery is set up.

-278.d: Bai Qi takes Ying, the Chu capital, and burns Yiling; Chu moves its capital to Chen, and Qin sets up Nan Commandery; Qu Yuan drowns himself in the Miluo.

-279.d: King Hui of Yan replaces Yue Yi with Qi Jie; Tian Dan crushes the Yan army with his fire-ox formation and recovers all of Qi. The same year Qin and Zhao meet at Mianchi, and Bai Qi floods the Chu town of Yan.

-284.d: The Yan general Yue Yi leads the armies of five states, Yan, Qin, Han, Zhao and Wei, to crush Qi west of the Ji River, taking more than seventy Qi towns in half a year; only Ju and Jimo hold out, and King Min of Qi dies at Ju. Song's lands are divided between Wei and Chu.

-286.d: King Min of Qi destroys Song (he had earlier styled himself Emperor of the East alongside King Zhao of Qin); Wei cedes Anyi to Qin. Qi is at the height of its power, which also alarms the other lords.

-290.d: Wei gives Qin four hundred li of Hedong, and Han two hundred li of Wusui; Qin has already taken Wan (291 BC), and the Nanyang basin passes to Qin.

-293.d: Bai Qi crushes the allied Han and Wei armies at Yique, beheading two hundred and forty thousand and capturing Gongsun Xi; the gate for Qin's advance east is thrown wide open.

-296.d: King Wuling of Zhao destroys Zhongshan, joining Dai and Handan into one. Qi, Han and Wei break through Hangu Pass, and Qin makes peace by returning Hewai and Wusui to Han, and Hewai and Fengling to Wei; King Huai of Chu dies while detained in Qin.

-300.d: Qi, Han and Wei crush Chu at Chuisha (301 BC), and Chu loses its land north of Wan and She; the Yan general Qin Kai drives the Donghu back more than a thousand li and Yan sets up five commanderies; King Wuling of Zhao crushes the Linhu and Loufan in the north and sets up Yunzhong and Yanmen.
-300.t: Battle of Chuisha · Yan drives back the Donghu

-306.d: King Huai of Chu sends Shao Hua into Yue to sow discord, destroys Yue in its internal turmoil, kills Wujiang, king of Yue, takes all the old lands of Wu up to the Zhe River and sets up Jiangdong Commandery (Yang Kuan's view). King Zhaoxiang of Qin comes to the throne, Queen Dowager Xuan and Wei Ran hold power, and Gan Mao urges the return of Wusui to Han.

-307.d: King Wu of Qin sends Gan Mao to take Yiyang from Han, beheading sixty thousand, to "open a road for chariots through the Three Rivers", and Qin "crosses the river and walls Wusui"; King Wu dies after breaking his kneecaps lifting a tripod. King Huai of Chu besieges Yongshi in Han again, and Qin sends troops to save Han. The same year King Wuling of Zhao orders the adoption of nomad dress and mounted archery.
-307.t: Qin takes Yiyang · nomad dress and mounted archery

-312.d: Deceived by Zhang Yi's "six hundred li of Shang and Wu", King Huai of Chu attacks Qin and is routed at Danyang; Qu Gai is captured, and Qin takes six hundred li of Hanzhong and sets up Hanzhong Commandery; the Chu army is defeated again at Lantian.

-316.d: Shu attacks Ju; the Marquis of Ju flees to Ba, and Ba and Ju appeal to Qin for help. King Huiwen of Qin follows Sima Cuo's advice, attacks and destroys Shu, then takes Ju and Ba, gaining the "Land of Abundance". Yue still holds Wu and Kuaiji, and the king of Yue will still send envoys to Wei as late as 312 BC. King Kuai of Yan cedes his throne to Zizhi, sowing the seeds of chaos in Yan.

-318.d: Gongsun Yan organises a vertical alliance of Wei, Zhao, Han, Yan and Chu against Qin, with King Huai of Chu as its head; it is defeated at Hangu Pass, and the next year Qin beheads eighty-two thousand at Xiuyu.

-323.d: Wei has also ceded the fifteen counties of Shang Commandery (328 BC); King Huiwen of Qin has assumed the title of king (325 BC) and captured Shan. In 323 BC Wei, Han, Zhao, Yan and Zhongshan recognise one another's royal titles; the same year Chu defeats Wei at Xiangling.
-323.t: Five states hail one another as kings

-330.d: Wei has already ceded Yinjin (332 BC); Gongsun Yan of Qin crushes Wei at Diaoyin, beheading eighty thousand, and Wei hands over all of Hexi. Qin's eastern border advances to the Yellow River.

-341.d: Sun Bin, strategist of the Qi army, uses the ruse of "reducing the cooking fires" to ambush the Wei army at Maling; Pang Juan cuts his own throat and Shen, crown prince of Wei, is captured. The next year Shang Yang exploits Wei's weakness to attack it and captures Prince Ang by a trick; Wei's hegemony collapses.

-350.d: King Hui of Wei dominates the Central Plains and has just moved his capital to Daliang; Duke Xiao of Qin has Shang Yang carry out his second reform and moves the capital to Xianyang; Yue still holds the old lands of Wu and Yue; Ba, Shu, Ju, Zhongshan, Song, Wey, Lu and the two Zhou all survive.
